title: Factcheck: No, Europe’s heatwaves are not being ‘caused’ by declining air pollution - Carbon Brief
gist: Carbon Brief factchecks Daily Telegraph and GB News headlines claiming a new study shows Europe's heatwaves are 'caused' by declining air pollution; scientists say the study actually shows greenhouse-gas warming drives the heatwaves while aerosol decline merely unmasked it via more sunlight and 'stuck' jet-stream patterns, and both the study and its coverage wrongly credit the Montreal Protocol for Europe's air-quality gains.

themes.theme: Media distorts the study into a net-zero attack line

insights.claim: The Daily Telegraph and GB News ran headlines stating European heatwaves are 'caused' by falling air pollution, a framing that multiple climate scientists interviewed by Carbon Brief say is incorrect.
insights.speaker: Robert McSweeney
insights.so_what: Shows how a nuanced attribution study gets flattened into a misleading causal claim in mainstream media, distorting the public debate around net-zero policy.
insights.quote: Heatwaves caused by fall in pollution.

insights.claim: Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice used the Telegraph's story to claim 'net stupid zero is contributing to rising temperatures, not helping' and that the public has been 'gaslit and lied to,' extending his existing rejection of CO2-driven warming.
insights.speaker: Richard Tice
insights.so_what: Illustrates how anti-net-zero political actors seize on misreported science to attack climate policy, a pattern worth tracking as a source of populist pressure on green regulation.
insights.quote: net stupid zero is contributing to rising temperatures, not helping... we have been gaslit and lied to

themes.theme: The actual mechanism: GHG warming masked by aerosols, unlocked via Rossby waves

insights.claim: ETH Zurich climate scientist Erich Fischer says heatwaves are caused by high-pressure systems that are now more frequent and intense because they occur in a climate that is far warmer than a century ago due to greenhouse-gas-induced warming, not by the aerosol decline itself.
insights.speaker: Erich Fischer
insights.so_what: Gives the correct causal chain investors and policymakers should use when evaluating heatwave narratives tied to net-zero politics: GHGs are the driver, aerosols were only masking it.
insights.quote: Heatwaves are caused by high-pressure systems and are now much more frequent and intense because they are happening in a climate that is much warmer than 100 years ago as a result of greenhouse-gas-induced warming.

insights.claim: A new Geophysical Research Letters study, using hundreds of simulations across nine climate models, finds that declining aerosol pollution is increasing the frequency of 'quasi-stationary' Rossby waves — jet-stream meanders that stall and trap weather systems over a region, prolonging heatwaves.
insights.speaker: Robert McSweeney
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, trackable atmospheric-circulation mechanism linking air-quality trends to European heatwave frequency, useful for following further attribution research.
insights.locator: Using hundreds of simulations from nine climate models

insights.claim: As European air quality improved through the second half of the 20th century, the loss of aerosols' historical cooling effect has boosted heatwaves both directly, by letting more sunlight reach the surface, and indirectly, by altering jet-stream behavior.
insights.speaker: Robert McSweeney
insights.so_what: Establishes the two distinct physical pathways by which cleaner air amplifies extreme heat, relevant to climate-risk and insurance modelers tracking European heat exposure.
insights.locator: As European countries improved their air quality

themes.theme: The study's own author and outside scientists push back on the causal claim

insights.claim: Study lead author Pedro Roldán‐Gómez of the Barcelona Supercomputer Centre states that 'most' of Europe's 'excess warming' relative to comparable northern-hemisphere regions can be linked to declining aerosols, but calls this a 'tricky point' that could be misread if not carefully explained, adding that greenhouse gases remain the most important factor overall.
insights.speaker: Pedro Roldán‐Gómez
insights.so_what: Shows the study's own author distancing from the media's oversimplified causal claim, a signal to discount secondary press coverage relative to the primary researcher's framing.
insights.quote: The contribution of greenhouse gases is, in any case, the most important factor.
insights.locator: Study lead author Dr Pedro Roldán‐Gómez

insights.claim: CICERO research professor Bjørn Samset argues it is 'simply wrong' to link the aerosol-driven heatwave findings to net-zero policy, since net-zero targets emerged decades after the cumulative air-pollution reductions the study examines.
insights.speaker: Bjørn Samset
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the political talking point tying clean-air science to net-zero costs, useful for assessing the credibility of anti-net-zero narratives in policy debate.

insights.claim: Samset states that 'nothing we do will change the fact that the consequences of global warming are due to human-induced CO2 emissions,' reaffirming that air pollution only temporarily moderates, and never causes or removes, global warming.
insights.speaker: Bjørn Samset
insights.so_what: Anchors the underlying scientific consensus that should override the misleading headline framing when assessing climate-attribution claims.
insights.quote: Air pollution never causes or removes global warming, it only temporarily moderates it.

insights.claim: Fischer notes that despite the aerosol-heatwave nuance, cutting air pollution remains highly desirable because the World Health Organisation estimates 7 million people still die prematurely each year from air pollution.
insights.speaker: Erich Fischer
insights.so_what: Reminds readers that the public-health case for clean-air policy is independent of, and far larger than, the heatwave-framing debate.
insights.quote: 7 million people still die prematurely every year due to air pollution.

insights.claim: Both the Daily Telegraph and the underlying study incorrectly attribute Europe's declining air pollution since the 1980s to the Montreal Protocol, which regulated ozone-depleting gases rather than air pollution — an error Samset calls 'glaring' and says should have been caught in peer review.
insights.speaker: Bjørn Samset
insights.so_what: Flags a factual gap in the underlying study itself, not just its media coverage, which should discount confidence in the paper's broader framing until corrected.
insights.quote: The Montreal Protocol did not deal with air pollution. It dealt with ozone-depleting gases and has been an extremely successful multi-national effort against environmental damage.

insights.claim: Study author Roldán‐Gómez responds to the Montreal Protocol criticism by conceding the protocol did not target aerosols directly but arguing it 'boosted the clean air policies' that followed.
insights.speaker: Pedro Roldán‐Gómez
insights.so_what: Shows the study author only partially conceding the error, which readers should weigh when judging how much the paper's aerosol-source narrative needs revision.
